figures.caption: Overview of our framework. We first use Gaussian centers to query multi-resolution feature grids to obtain features. Then, together with view directions, we employ an MLP to predict view-dependent colors for each Gaussian. The predicted colors and Gaussian attributes are then rendered by the differentiable rasterizer. We impose self-learned supervision on the neural color field.

citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 1, we learn 3D Gaussians $\{\bm{G}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J}$ (with center $\bm{m}_{j}$, opacity $o_{j}$, scale $s_{j}$, color $\bm{c}_{j}$) from RGB images $\{\bm{V}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{I}$ via 3DGS.

We therefore sample points along each ray around the intersection, as shown in Fig. 2, and constrain their colors to be zero.

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a vital tool in novel view synthesis. 3D Gaussian functions with attributes like color, opacity, and scale are stacked together to explicitly model a radiance field. However, discrete 3D Gaussians usually produce poor depth with few geometry details but lots of floaters, which hinders the effective modeling of smooth radiance fields. To address this issue, we propose to learn a radiance field within a continuous view-dependent color field parameterized by neural networks. With continuous constraints in color, the bias on low-frequency signals of neural networks can highly encourage the geometry modeling to contribute to high-frequency color variations on images, getting rid of solely relying on the color attribute itself. Moreover, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of the neural color field, making large changes of each Gaussian’s color also match with large changes of its position in terms of a ratio. To this end, we additionally introduce novel self-learning strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field without any external knowledge or priors, aiming for better generalization on unseen scenes. Our numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks justify our idea and show better ability of high fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS. Project page: https://github.com/yangyixi21/Neural-Color-Fields-3DGS.

sections.body: The paper argues that discrete 3DGS Gaussians fit high-frequency color poorly, which yields rough geometry and floaters. Earlier fixes add geometry constraints such as distance fields, multi-view consistency, or monocular priors. The text names drawbacks for each: sensitive distance-to-density mappings, costly multi-view checks, or limited generalization from external priors. The proposed approach predicts each Gaussian's color with a neural network inside a continuous view-dependent color field. The network's low-frequency bias and a Lipschitz constraint are meant to push geometry to explain high-frequency color changes. Self-learning supervision needs no external priors or data-driven strategy. The stated contributions are the color-field formulation, the self-supervision, and benchmark results.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Discrete Gaussians often fit geometry poorly, so the method constrains their colors within a smooth neural color field.

sections.body: The section groups related work into three areas. First, geometry methods for 3DGS: 2DGS flattens Gaussians into planes, PGSR adds depth and multi-view constraints, GSPrior derives priors from a TSDF grid, and SuGaR aligns Gaussians with the surface. Second, neural implicit fields, which the text says favor low frequencies, and Lipschitz continuity, which the text says prevents disproportionate output changes. Third, PermutoSDF, which limits color field variation to push high-frequency signals into geometric structures. The authors state that their approach differs by constraining the neural color field's Lipschitz constant directly, so large color variations correspond to significant geometric changes.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior 3DGS geometry methods use constraints or priors, while neural fields' low-frequency bias suggests a geometric regularizer.

sections.body:
The method learns 3D Gaussians from RGB images and a hash feature grid whose features feed a neural network. Each Gaussian's view-dependent color is

$$
\mathbf{c}_{j}^{r}=F(\mathbf{f}_{j},\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\mathbf{f}_{j}$ is the grid feature at the Gaussian center and $\mathbf{r}$ is the normalized view direction. Training combines the rendering loss with on-surface color supervision from back-projected depth, zero-color constraints before and behind the surface, and a Lipschitz term built from per-layer bounds. The tetrahedral lattice needs four corners per cell instead of eight, which the text says reduces storage and computation by a factor of two. The color field applies only to Gaussians inside a 3D bounding box, and gradient detachment stops 3D losses from updating Gaussian attributes.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Each Gaussian's color comes from a hash grid and network, trained with rendering loss plus surface, free-space and Lipschitz terms.

sections.body: The evaluation uses an object-level benchmark (DTU), a large-scale benchmark (TnT), and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes. Geometry is scored with Chamfer Distance (CD) on DTU and F-score on TnT; rendering uses PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS. On DTU, the text reports average CD improvements of 30.0% over FastGS, 41.1% over 3DGS and 3.8% over 2DGS, and PGSR's average CD falls from 0.53 to 0.51. Rendering on DTU is comparable: Ours(3DGS) reaches 32.77 PSNR against 32.56 for 3DGS. On Mip-NeRF 360 outdoor scenes, Ours(3DGS) PSNR is 24.44 against 24.64 for 3DGS, a small reduction the appendix describes as a rendering-quality trade-off. The authors state that gains are smaller on backbones with strong geometry constraints.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across object-level and large-scale benchmarks, the method improves geometry for several 3DGS backbones with mixed rendering results.

sections.body: The conclusion says the method constrains smoothness in the radiance field to improve geometry inference with 3DGS. It attributes this to the spectral bias of the neural network together with Lipschitz regularization, which encourages geometry to align with color variation. It states that the self-learning strategy needs no external priors and that experiments show superior geometry reconstruction over recent 3DGS variants. It also says the method maintains rendering quality. The appendix qualifies that claim: outdoor rendering shows a small reduction in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS for 3DGS. The appendix also says the geometric evidence for outdoor scenes remains qualitative, because no ground-truth geometry evaluation is given there.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The method improves 3DGS geometry without external priors, though the appendix notes a small rendering reduction on outdoor scenes.

sections.body: The appendix has four lettered parts. Appendix B gives implementation details: a bounding box selects Gaussians that use the neural color field, and depth is normalized by accumulated opacity, with pixels kept only when opacity exceeds 0.1. Appendix C reports that Lipschitz regularization lowers average Chamfer Distance from 1.29 to 1.23 on DTU and sets front and back sampling variances to 0.1 and 0.01. Appendix D discusses outdoor rendering trade-offs, a reflective region where Lip-only lowers local CD from 7.5207 to 7.2516 mm, smaller gains on strong backbones, and runtime overhead. It states the color network cannot be fused into the rasterization pipeline and adds memory cost. Appendix E links the code repository.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers implementation details, extra ablations, depth normalization, outdoor and reflective-region analyses, and limitations.
